articles.title: Cytologic Diagnosis of Large B-Cell Lymphoma: Diagnostic Approach and Differential Diagnosis.
articles.abstract: Large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) encompasses a diverse group of aggressive lymphoid neoplasms, the most common of which is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). A precise diagnosis is critical for determining prognosis and therapeutic strategies, particularly as new molecular subtypes and classification criteria have been introduced in the 5th edition of the World Health Organization (WHO) classification of hematolymphoid tumors (WHO-HAEM5, 2022). Fine needle aspiration cytology is a safe and minimally invasive diagnostic tool for assessing lymphadenopathy and extranodal masses. LBCLs are typically characterized by single cells with large nuclei, vesicular chromatin pattern, and prominent nucleoli. The diagnosis of LBCL and the distinction distinguishing between LBCL subtypes requires the integration of cytomorphologic features with ancillary techniques, including immunocytochemistry, flow cytometry, fluorescence in situ hybridization, and next-generation sequencing. This review synthesizes the cytologic features, immunophenotypic profiles, molecular signatures, and clinical implications of LBCL subtypes, highlighting recent advances in cytopathology and classification.

articles.title: Circulating alpha-fetoprotein-specific T-cell responses are associated with clinical outcomes after radiofrequency ablation or immunotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Circulating tumor antigen-specific T-cell responses are promising peripheral immune biomarkers associated with treatment efficacy, yet clinical translation is hampered by incomplete epitope maps and non-standardized assays. This study aimed to map the T-cell epitope repertoire of AFP and develop a PBMC-based assay to quantify circulating AFP-specific T-cell responses in HCC. CD8+ T-cell epitopes in AFP were screened using in silico prediction, peptide-PBMC coculture, peptide competitive binding assays, and immunization in HLA-transgenic mice, and then applied in clinical cohorts. Totally, 48 CD8+ T-cell epitopes identified here and 20 from our previous study were confirmed immunogenic. These peptides were used to establish an IFN-γ ELISpot assay for quantifying circulating AFP-specific T-cell responses in PBMCs. A total of 170 HCC patients with elevated serum AFP were included in two derivation cohorts: 80 patients treated with RFA and 90 receiving anti-PD-1 plus anti-VEGF therapy. In the RFA derivation cohort, the post-treatment/pre-treatment fold of AFP-specific T-cell responses was independently associated with DFS (AUC, 0.838; cutoff, 1.95-fold for DFS >12 vs. ≤12 mo). In the anti-PD-1 plus anti-VEGF derivation cohort, the post-treatment/pre-treatment fold of AFP-specific T-cell responses was independently associated with objective response and 6-month PFS (AUC, 0.850 and 0.863, respectively), with a unified 2.5-fold cutoff for outcome stratification. These findings in the immunotherapy setting were further validated in an independent external cohort of 50 HCC patients with elevated serum AFP receiving combined anti-PD-1 and anti-VEGF therapy. This study establishes an IFN-γ ELISpot assay for quantifying circulating AFP-specific T-cell responses in PBMCs and supports their potential translational utility as a novel peripheral immune-monitoring biomarker associated with clinical outcomes in AFP-positive HCC patients.

articles.title: Gut Microbiota and Neuroendocrine Neoplasms: Emerging Insights into the Gut-Metabolome-Immune Axis.
articles.abstract: Neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs) are heterogeneous tumors with increasing incidence and substantial clinical variability. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiota may influence NEN biology through immune, metabolic, and tumor microenvironment interactions. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood Methods: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on microbiota alterations across NEN subtypes, integrating microbiome profiling, intratumoral microbiome studies, multi-omics analyses, and Mendelian randomization (MR) investigations exploring potential causal associations and mediating pathways. Patients with NENs consistently exhibit gut microbial dysbiosis, although signatures vary by tumor site. Evidence of an intratumoral microbiome in NENs suggests that bacteria may be integrated into the tumor microenvironment, potentially influencing immune regulation and tumor behavior. Multi-omics studies further demonstrate systemic metabolic alterations, including dysregulated tryptophan metabolism, altered circulating organic acids, and increased microbial-derived uremic toxins associated with metastatic disease. Mendelian randomization analyses support potential bidirectional causal relationships between gut microbiota and gastroenteropancreatic NENs, with evidence of immune- and metabolite-mediated effects. Importantly, microbiota involvement appears heterogeneous across NENs subtypes, reflecting tissue-specific ecological and hormonal contexts. Chronic inflammation may further link dysbiosis and tumorigenesis, contributing to a shared pathogenic continuum. The gut microbiota is emerging as a potential area of interest in NEN biology, with possible links to interconnected microbial, metabolic, and immune pathways. Although the underlying mechanisms and causal relationships remain to be established, current evidence suggests potential interactions between the host-microbiome axis and tumor development and progression. Further studies are needed to clarify these relationships and assess the potential of microbiota-based biomarkers and therapeutic strategies in NENs.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy combined with palliative transarterial chemoembolization followed by targeted therapy and immunotherapy in patients with BCLC stage C hepatocellular carcinoma: Clinical trial protocol.
articles.abstract: Interventional therapy combined with systemic treatment has demonstrated promising antitumor activity and an overall manageable safety profile in patients with advanced, unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, prospective evidence supporting the optimal combination strategy remains limited, and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) characteristics underlying differential treatment responses have not been systematically elucidated. The present study aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) combined with palliative transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), followed by sequential targeted-immunotherapy, in treatment-naïve patients with BCLC stage C HCC, while also exploring the TIME features associated with therapeutic response. This study is a prospective, single-arm, phase II clinical trial that will enroll treatment-naïve patients with BCLC C HCC who are unsuitable for surgical resection. Tumor tissue and peripheral blood samples will be collected at baseline prior to treatment initiation. All patients will receive HAIC with a modified FOLFOX regimen combined with palliative TACE. Immediately after the interventional procedure, patients will undergo intra-arterial infusion of bevacizumab (200-300 mg) and intravenous administration of sintilimab (200 mg) every three weeks for a total of six cycles. After two treatment cycles, patients will be stratified according to their treatment response, and five additional tumor tissue and blood samples will be collected from each group. Upon completion of local therapy, patients will continue with maintenance therapy consisting of intravenous bevacizumab (15 mg/kg) and sintilimab (200 mg) every three weeks until disease progression or the development of intolerable toxicity. This study will evaluate the efficacy and safety of HAIC combined with palliative TACE followed by sequential targeted-immunotherapy and explore TIME features associated with treatment response. The findings may provide evidence to inform multimodal treatment strategies and personalized therapy for advanced HCC. ChiCTR2500115704.

articles.title: Maintaining integrity amidst turmoil: A qualitative exploration of parental coping process during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for pediatric cancer.
articles.abstract: Childhood cancer, particularly pediatric hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), imposes profound psychosocial and socioeconomic challenges on parents. This study aimed to develop a grounded theory explaining the dynamic coping process experienced by parents during their child's HSCT journey. This qualitative study used Corbin and Strauss's (2015) grounded theory approach to develop an explanatory account of the parental coping process during pediatric HSCT. Twenty Persian-speaking parents of children undergoing HSCT at a tertiary care center in Iran were recruited through purposive and theoretical sampling. Data collection began with unstructured interviews and progressed to in-depth semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed through constant comparative analysis, including open, axial, and selective coding. Parental coping during pediatric HSCT was a multifaceted, non-linear process shaped by evolving stressors and adaptive responses. The analysis generated a grounded theory centered on the core category, "maintaining integrity amidst turmoil," which reflected parents' efforts to manage their central concern, "entrapment in adversity," arising from perceived threats and trapped in suffering. Coping was mediated through two key strategies: "health-seeking behaviors" and "emotional and cognitive coping efforts". Contextual factors, including a "continuum of support systems" (ranging from empowering healthcare interactions to systemic inadequacies) and "beliefs and individual situation" (cultural, spiritual, and personal values), significantly influenced coping trajectories. Outcomes included "relative adaptation" and "self-actualization". Tailored support systems that address systemic gaps and cultural beliefs are essential for fostering adaptive coping. Strengthening health-seeking and emotional-cognitive strategies can promote functional stability and personal growth among parents.

articles.title: Senolytic drug reduces cancer resistance to PD-L1 blockade.
articles.abstract: Resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), including anti-PD-L1 therapies, remains a major challenge in cancer treatment, with many patients relapsing despite initial responses. Here, we develop a mathematical model to investigate a mechanism of anti-PD-L1 resistance driven by age-associated senescence of CD8+ T cells, in which senescent T cells (Ts) secrete VEGF, thereby promoting tumor growth through enhanced vascular support. To counteract this effect, we incorporate the senolytic drug navitoclax (ABT-263), which selectively eliminates senescent T cells, and evaluate the efficacy of combined senolytic-anti-PD-L1 therapy in extending tumor remission. Model predictions are validated against independent murine data involving navitoclax and anti-PD-L1 treatment. The model is used to study different strategies of combining the senolytic drug with anti-PD-L1, in order to maximize the remission time of the combined treatment. The optimal starting time of the treatment with the senolytic drug depends on the senescent-to-functional T cells ratio, Ts/T. The paper identifies immune senescence as an important determinant of response to cancer immunotherapy.

articles.title: GPCR-Gαq signaling drives adaptive resistance to MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma.
articles.abstract: Oncogenic BRAFV600E mutations drive constitutive MAPK signaling across various cancers; however, resistance to MEK inhibitors such as trametinib undermines clinical benefits, and the mechanisms sustaining MAPK activity under treatment remain unclear. We developed a lin-45(V627E) Caenorhabditis elegans model to mimic oncogenic BRAF signaling and found that these animals exhibited high-dose trametinib resistance, as assessed by brood size. Transcriptomic analysis revealed increased egl-30 expression in worms resistant to high-dose trametinib. Genetic and pharmacological analyses implicated EGL-30/Gαq-PLC-PKC signaling in this high-dose resistance phenotype. In trametinib-resistant A375 melanoma cells, F2RL1, which encodes the Gαq-coupled GPCR PAR2, was upregulated compared with parental cells. Functional inhibition of PAR2 or downstream Gαq signaling reduced ERK phosphorylation and impaired the viability of trametinib-resistant melanoma cells. Furthermore, combined inhibition of MEK and Gαq-PLC-PKC signaling synergistically suppresses tumor growth and restores trametinib sensitivity in xenograft models. These findings uncover Gαq-associated signaling as a conserved contributor to trametinib resistance and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in BRAF-mutant melanoma.

articles.title: Identification and structural characterization of MMP1 and MMP9 as potential targets of curcumin and resveratrol in lung adenocarcinoma.
articles.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a major subtype of lung cancer characterized by substantial molecular heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Curcumin and resveratrol are naturally occurring bioactive compounds with reported anticancer activities, but their potential molecular targets and mechanisms in LUAD remain incompletely characterized. This study aimed to systematically identify and characterize potential molecular targets of curcumin and resveratrol in LUAD using an integrated computational framework. Potential targets of curcumin and resveratrol were collected from multiple compound-target databases and integrated with LUAD-associated genes obtained from GeneCards and OMIM. Shared targets were evaluated using protein-protein interaction analysis and network-based prioritization. Transcriptomic and clinical validation was performed using The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-LUAD dataset, including differential expression, diagnostic performance, survival analysis, mutation profiling, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), immune association, immune checkpoint correlation, and co-expression analysis. Structurally prioritized targets were subsequently investigated using molecular docking, interaction profiling, and redocking validation, followed by molecular dynamics and binding free energy analyses. The integrated target-screening strategy identified 976 unique targets for curcumin, 6,897 targets for resveratrol, and 3,885 LUAD-associated targets, with 325 common targets between curcumin, resveratrol, and LUAD. Downstream investigation of potential targets identified MMP1 and MMP9 from network and multi-level evidence prioritization. Both genes demonstrated diagnostic potential in TCGA-LUAD, with MMP1 achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.9281 (95% CI: 0.8785-0.9776) and MMP9 an AUC of 0.8466 (95% CI: 0.7727-0.9205). However, MMP1 and MMP9 were not independently related to overall survival in stage-adjusted survival analysis models. Functional enrichment analysis identified biological pathways associated with the expression profiles of MMP1 and MMP9, while immune cells, immune checkpoint, and gene co-expression analyses indicated broader molecular and immune associations. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable predicted binding of curcumin and resveratrol to MMP1 and MMP9, with docking scores ranging from -7.0 to -9.9 kcal/mol. Mutation analysis further identified an MMP1 p.R214S variant at a residue corresponding to ARG214 involved in the predicted resveratrol interaction, suggesting a potentially relevant structural association. Molecular dynamics and MM/GBSA analysis showed that the selected complexes are stable and energetically favorable. DFT calculation indicated different electronic properties of both the compounds, ADMET analysis demonstrated good drug like properties for both compounds, complying the Lipinski's Rule of Five. Overall, this integrated computational analysis identified MMP1, and MMP9 as potential molecular targets associated with curcumin and resveratrol in LUAD. The combined structural, dynamic, electronic, pharmacokinetic, and toxicity evaluations provide a comprehensive framework for prioritizing these compounds and targets for further experimental investigation.

articles.title: Bevacizumab and thrombosis risk in cancer patients with COVID-19: A national retrospective cohort study (TIC-TAC).
articles.abstract: Cancer patients treated with bevacizumab are at increased risk of thromboembolic events. COVID-19 is also associated with thromboembolism, but its impact on thromboembolic risk in cancer patients receiving bevacizumab remains unclear. The TIC-TAC study aimed to assess whether COVID-19 diagnosis is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolic events (VTE) within 30 days or arterial (ATE) thromboembolic events within 90 days in this population. A retrospective nationwide cohort study was conducted using the French national health data system. Cancer patients treated with bevacizumab between January 2019 and December 2021 were included. Bevacizumab exposures were used as statistical unit, and defined to 5 half-lives (100 days) after its administration. COVID-19 diagnosis was defined by ICD-10 codes or positive virological tests. The primary outcome was the occurrence of VTE or ATE during hospitalization. Cox models with time-dependent exposure and Fine and Gray competing-risk models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and subdistribution hazard ratios (SHR), with death considered as a competing risk. Among 58,855 patients (median age 67 years, 79.9% with metastatic disease), 5,589 VTE and 1,926 ATE were recorded over 46,750 and 46,915 person-years, respectively. COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with a higher risk of VTE within 30 days after diagnosis in crude (HR 1.89, 95% CI 1.55-2.29) and adjusted Cox models (aHR 1.99 [1.64-2.43]), as well as in the Fine and Gray model (aSHR 1.70 [1.40-2.07]). However, the unadjusted absolute risk increase was modest: one additional VTE per 64.6 person-months of COVID-19 exposure. A significant interaction between COVID-19 diagnosis and anticoagulant therapy was observed in the VTE Cox model (p = 0.007), but not in the Fine and Gray model. No significant association was found between COVID-19 diagnosis and ATE risk. The study showed that 30 days period after a COVID-19 diagnosis could be associated with an increased risk of VTE in cancer patients treated with bevacizumab. However, the absolute risk difference, although unadjusted and therefore uncertain, appeared modest. Causality cannot be established in this retrospective design. No significant association was observed for ATE.

articles.title: Factors Associated With Radiation Pneumonitis and Prognosis in Esophageal Cancer Patients Undergoing Radiotherapy.
articles.journal: Cancer control : journal of the Moffitt Cancer Center
articles.abstract: IntroductionRadiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is one of the most severe complications in esophageal cancer (EC) patients undergoing radiotherapy. However, the risk factors for acute radiation pneumonitis (RP) have not been fully clarified. This study aimed to explore the factors associated to RP induced by precise radiotherapy and the prognosis of EC patients.MethodsThis single-center retrospective observational study enrolled 101 EC patients who underwent radiotherapy for primary lesions and/or mediastinal metastatic lymph nodes. The relationships between clinical characteristics, dosimetric parameters, hematological markers of inflammation, and the occurrence of RP were analyzed. The cutoff values were determined by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Multivariable logistic regression and Kaplan-Meier methods were also performed to investigate the prognostic role of these factors.ResultsThe incidence rate of RP in this study was 47.52%, but most cases (75%) suffered grade 1 RP. Univariate analysis indicated that neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), systemic immune-inflammatory index (SII), system inflammation response index (SIRI), V5, V10, V15, V20, V25, V30, and lung mean dose (Dmean) affected the occurrence of RP. Multivariate logistic regression analysis identified SII, SIRI, and V20 as independent risk factors for RP in EC patients. articles.title: Lactate-rich tumor employs the KAT5-HIF1α axis to modulate the activity of the hypoxia pathway and facilitates tumor progression.
articles.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
articles.abstract: Substantial evidence shows that hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) up-regulates glycolytic enzymes and promotes lactate production, which contributes to "Warburg Effect." Nevertheless, the impact of lactate or lactylation modification on hypoxia signaling pathways within the tumor microenvironment remains largely unclear. Here, we report that lactate can induce the upregulation of hypoxia pathway activity in a HIF1α-dependent manner. We identified that KAT5 as a lysine lactyltransferase of HIF1α and the "writer" responsible for lactylation at HIF1α K389, K460, K674, and K682, and HDAC2 as a HIF1α de-lactylase. articles.title: Personalized
articles.journal: Radiographics : a review publication of the Radiological Society of North America, Inc
articles.abstract: Yttrium 90 transarterial radioembolization has evolved from a palliative lobar therapy for advanced liver malignancies into a versatile potentially curative treatment across hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) stages, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), and liver metastases. Central to this evolution is the shift from empirical population-based activity prescriptions to personalized dosimetry, tailoring administered activity to each patient's anatomy, tumor biology, treatment intent, and microsphere distribution to optimize tumor absorbed dose while constraining normal tissue exposure. Prospective studies have demonstrated that personalized dosimetry significantly improves tumor response and overall survival compared with conventional dosing. Despite this evidence, clinical adoption remains inconsistent. In this review, the authors aim to address that gap by providing a practical intent-based framework for implementation. They present dosimetric principles, activity prescription methods, and dose-response evidence across HCC, iCCA, and liver metastases, with practical recommendations organized by treatment intent. Treatment intent, whether curative or palliative, is the primary determinant of dosimetric strategy, guiding selection of the dosimetry model, target dose, and normal liver dose constraints. The authors review pretreatment planning work flows and posttreatment verification and present a practical decision algorithm integrating clinical intent, imaging, and dosimetry modeling.

articles.title: Transcriptional analyses of patient derived xenograft models reveal distinct subsets of small cell lung cancer.
articles.abstract: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a neuroendocrine carcinoma characterized by early metastasis, rapid emergence of therapy resistance, and dismal patient outcomes. SCLC subtypes have been proposed based on expression of lineage transcription factors ASCL1, NEUROD1, and POU2F3 and the level of inflammation. To further discern biologically distinct subsets, we apply non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) to gene expression data from 146 SCLC patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. We identify three ASCL1-dominant and three NEUROD1-dominant subsets, an ASCL1/NEUROD1 co-active subset, and a REST-active low-neuroendocrine subset. These subsets differ in MYC family expression, transcription factor activation, antigen presentation transcriptional programs, and expression of cell surface molecules that represent therapeutic targets. Using a random forest classifier, we project these clusters onto 7 genetic mouse models of SCLC, human cell lines, and patient data from the IMpower133 clinical trial, allowing us to link PDX-derived subsets to specific murine and cellular models and to patient responses.

articles.title: OSTM1 restrains B-cell lymphomagenesis by promoting PDE3B degradation and activating cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling.
articles.abstract: Through a genome-wide forward CRISPR/Cas9 screen in interleukin-3 (IL3)-dependent Ba/F3 cells, we identified osteoclastogenesis-associated transmembrane protein 1 (OSTM1) as a previously unrecognized tumor suppressor. Analysis of patient datasets revealed that OSTM1 is frequently deleted or downregulated in human B-cell malignancies (BCM). In mice, Cd19-Cre-driven B cell-specific monoallelic or biallelic deletion of Ostm1 cooperated with Cdkn2a loss to drive lymphomagenesis with near-complete penetrance. Mechanistically, OSTM1 directly interacts with phosphodiesterase 3B (PDE3B) and promotes its proteasomal degradation. Because PDE3B hydrolyzes cyclic AMP (cAMP), loss of OSTM1 stabilizes PDE3B, leading to suppression of tumor-suppressive cAMP-dependent PKA/CREB signaling and promotion of oncogenic transformation. Consistent with this mechanism, PDE3B is frequently amplified or upregulated in BCM, and expression of CREB/CREBBP transcriptional targets correlates positively with OSTM1 expression but inversely with PDE3B across BCM cohorts. Importantly, silencing Pde3b reverses oncogenic transformation driven by Ostm1 loss. Together, these findings establish OSTM1 as a tumor suppressor and uncover an OSTM1/PDE3B/cAMP signaling axis that restrains B-cell lymphomagenesis and may represent a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.

articles.title: Targeting CGRP signaling reverses maladaptive neurogenic immunosuppression in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma models.
articles.abstract: Neurogenic inflammation is one component that sculpts the immune milieu of solid tumors. However, it remains unclear how the sensory-neuroimmune axis shapes the immune microenvironment in cold tumors to bolster treatment resistance. Using orthotopic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) models, we demonstrate tumor growth-induced sensory hyperexcitability, and that surgical sensory signaling interruption reduced tumor growth. Genetic knockout of a key neuropeptide released by sensory neurons, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), encoded by Calca, produced eradication when paired with radioimmunotherapy. Such treatment reduced Treg infiltration and immunosuppressive function in Calca knockout mice. We also observed that high-dose psilocybin functions as a CGRP inhibitor and transiently reduces tumor growth by increasing antitumor immunity. Additionally, psilocybin increased circulating serotonin, which was partially reversed with platelet activation inhibitor, clopidogrel. We observed differential effects on CD8 and Treg functionality by psilocin in vitro. Correlational analyses in plasma from human subjects following a single-dose psilocybin corroborated these findings. Together, this work underscores the complex interaction of neurogenic inflammation and the tumor immune microenvironment, highlighting a potential therapeutic avenue for HNSCC and other solid tumors.

articles.title: Metastatic Prostate Cancer Treatment Variation in Veterans.
articles.abstract: Not all men with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) receive the recommended combination therapy of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) plus an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) and/or chemotherapy. To determine factors associated with combination therapy use among veterans with mCSPC in the national Veterans Health Administration (VHA) system. This cohort study included US veterans diagnosed with mCSPC between January 1, 2023, through December 31, 2024, who were followed up through June 30, 2025. National multicenter data were obtained from the VHA electronic health record, community care settings (private care paid with VHA benefits), and Medicare. All included veterans were identified through a validated natural language processing algorithm, were followed up in the VHA for at least 2 years prior to their metastatic diagnosis, were provided ADT within the first 6 months of diagnosis, and received no prostate cancer-directed therapy in the year prior to diagnosis. Clinical factors (eg, comorbidities, frailty, prostate cancer burden at diagnosis) and nonclinical factors (eg, annual household income, neighborhood disadvantage) were investigated to determine their association with the outcome. The primary outcome was receipt of combination therapy (ie, ADT plus ARPI [abiraterone, enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide] and/or docetaxel) vs ADT alone. Information on these treatments was obtained through pharmacy records. Multilevel logistic regression models were used and marginal predicted probabilities were reported to determine the associations of factors with receipt of combination therapy. Variation among VHA facilities was reported. A total of 4023 veterans (mean [SD] age, 75.3 [8.0] years) met eligibility criteria. Of these patients, 2339 (58.1%) had de novo metastatic disease, while 1684 (41.9%) had recurrent disease. Overall, 2564 patients (63.7%) received combination therapy. In adjusted analyses, older veterans (eg, aged 85-89 years: predicted probability, -14.1 [95% CI, -20.5 to -8.2] percentage points [pp]) and veterans with more comorbidities (eg, congestive heart failure: predicted probability, -7.5 [95% CI, -12.9 to -2.5] pp) were less likely to receive combination therapy. Annual household income and neighborhood disadvantage were not associated with receipt of combination therapy. Patients treated by urologists were less likely to receive combination therapy than patients treated by hematologist-oncologists (predicted probability, -23.7 [95% CI, -27.4 to -19.6] pp). Use of combination therapy ranged from 34% to 78% among VHA facilities. In this cohort study of veterans with de novo and recurrent mCSPC, receipt of combination therapy was high; annual household income and neighborhood disadvantage had no association with treatment use. The study findings suggest that the region where a veteran lives, the facility where they receive care, and the type of cancer specialist they see are factors of the variation in combination therapy use that need further exploration.

articles.title: Functional precision medicine in leukemias: current applications, challenges, and future directions.
articles.abstract: Functional precision medicine represents a promising approach to address the biological heterogeneity and therapeutic complexity of leukemias. By integrating direct functional assessment of drug response with molecular and clinical information, this strategy provides a more comprehensive framework for individualized therapy selection. Although important challenges remain, including methodological standardization, limited viability of primary leukemic cells, high infrastructure costs, and the need for prospective clinical validation, ongoing technological and computational advances are expected to facilitate broader clinical implementation. Ultimately, functional precision medicine may become a central component of modern hematologic oncology, enabling more dynamic, biologically informed, and patient-centered therapeutic strategies.

articles.title: Oncolytic vaccinia virus targeting HSP70 exhibits significant cytotoxic effects on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), known as the king of cancers, has very limited treatment options and drugs. Oncolytic viruses have been used in tumor biologic therapy, but their therapeutic efficacy is restricted due to low replication levels within tumor cells. Recently, we constructed a novel recombinant oncolytic vaccinia virus (oncoVV-shHSP70) by homologous recombination of HSP70 shRNA into the TK region, which exhibited strong replication capability and cytotoxicity in PDAC. Preliminary mechanistic studies suggested that oncoVV-shHSP70 may elevate ROS levels by inhibiting activation of the NRF2/HO-1 antioxidant pathway, thereby triggering the caspase cascade and inducing apoptosis. Additionally, the virus modulated transcription levels of cytokine-related genes. In BALB/c nude mouse models, oncoVV-shHSP70 significantly suppressed tumor growth, demonstrating potent antitumor activity. In C57BL/6 immunocompetent mice, oncoVV-shHSP70 was preliminarily found to increase CD8⁺ T cell infiltration. The results of this study support the potential of oncoVV-shHSP70 as a novel strategy for PDAC, warranting further investigation.

articles.title: Vulvar Paget Disease: From Empirical Management to Emerging Precision Oncology Strategies.
articles.abstract: Extramammary Paget disease (EMPD) is a rare cutaneous adenocarcinoma arising in apocrine gland-bearing skin, most commonly affecting the vulva. While non-invasive disease generally follows an indolent course with favorable prognosis, invasive locoregionally advanced or metastatic EMPD remains a major therapeutic challenge because of poor outcomes, lack of disease-specific guidelines, and limited efficacy of conventional systemic therapies. This unmet need supports a shift from empirical treatment toward biologically informed strategies. We performed a narrative review of PubMed and clinical trial registries to evaluate current therapies and emerging molecularly driven approaches, with particular focus on vulvar Paget disease (VPD). Available evidence suggests that conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy offers only temporary disease control with limited durable benefit. In contrast, recent molecular and immunological discoveries are reshaping the therapeutic landscape. HER2 currently represents the most clinically actionable target, supported by a strong biological rationale, multiple clinical reports, and the best prospective evidence available to date. Other potential targets include immune-related biomarkers, steroid hormone receptor signaling, GLUT1, NECTIN4, tumor mutational burden, and selected histology-agnostic genomic alterations, highlighting the marked biological heterogeneity of EMPD. However, most evidence remains preclinical or derives from small case series. Immune checkpoint inhibitors have shown sporadic but clinically meaningful activity in selected patients, particularly in tumors with high tumor mutational burden, supporting biomarker-driven immunotherapeutic strategies. Advanced EMPD should be regarded not simply as a rare chemoresistant malignancy, but as a biologically heterogeneous disease requiring comprehensive pathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular characterization to guide future precision-based therapies.

articles.title: Ultra-short-term in-hospital multimodal prehabilitation in older patients undergoing laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer: a randomized controlled trial.
articles.journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
articles.abstract: Prehabilitation has emerged as a promising supportive care strategy to improve surgical outcomes; however, evidence regarding ultra-short-term interventions in elderly gastric cancer patients remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and feasibility of a short-term (6-8 days) in-hospital multimodal prehabilitation program on functional recovery and postoperative outcomes. In this single-center, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial, 76 patients aged ≥ 60 years undergoing elective laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer were randomized (1:1) to in-hospital prehabilitation or standard care. The intervention included supervised exercise, individualized nutritional support, and psychological optimization delivered during the 6-8 days of preoperative hospitalization. The primary outcome was change in 6-min walking distance (6MWD) at 28-35 days postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included postoperative complications, recovery milestones, length of stay, and patient-reported outcomes (QoR-15 and HADS). Analyses were performed on a modified intention-to-treat population. A total of 70 patients were included in the final analysis (prehabilitation: n = 34; control: n = 36). Adherence was high (exercise 98.0%, oral nutritional supplements 95.6%, psychological support 98.4% of planned sessions or servings). From baseline to the preoperative assessment, the 6MWD increased in the prehabilitation group (+ 31.53 ± 14.70 m) but declined in the control group (- 2.19 ± 15.98 m; P < 0.001). At 28-35 days postoperatively, the prehabilitation group demonstrated preserved or improved functional capacity compared with the control group, which showed a significant decline (Δ6MWD: + 6.00 ± 15.48 m vs. - 26.20 ± 13.34 m; P < 0.001). In exploratory analyses, postoperative complications were less frequent in the prehabilitation group (11.8% vs. 38.9%, P = 0.009), mainly owing to pulmonary infection (8.8% vs. 30.6%) and Clavien-Dindo grade I-II events; severe complications (grade ≥ III) did not differ significantly (2.9% vs. 8.3%, P = 0.615). Patients in the prehabilitation group achieved earlier milestones for postoperative ambulation, return of flatus, and resumption of oral intake (all P < 0.001) and had a shorter postoperative stay (10.06 ± 2.97 vs. 13.31 ± 6.34 days, P = 0.008), but a longer preoperative stay (8.71 ± 2.75 vs. 4.97 ± 2.93 days) and no difference in total hospital stay (19.76 vs. 19.28 days, P = 0.739). QoR-15 scores were significantly higher in the prehabilitation group during early recovery, while no between-group differences were observed in HADS scores. In-hospital multimodal prehabilitation lasting 6-8 days appeared feasible and was associated with better functional capacity and, in exploratory analyses, fewer postoperative complications in older patients undergoing laparoscopic gastrectomy for gastric cancer. Recovery milestones were assessed without blinding of care providers, total hospital stay was unchanged, and no economic evaluation was performed. Larger multicenter trials are needed to confirm these findings. Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR), ChiCTR2300070553, registered on 17 April 2023.
